title: Lena and the Room
premise: Oscar Ashgrove hosts a late-night call-in show whose callers all died the previous week, and for fifteen years has rationalized every anomaly in the house they inherited. When mirrors begin lagging a second behind reality, Oscar learns the house is a room that was stolen in 1974 from a family who never stopped looking for it, and that the last living descendant, Marisol Vane, arrives to sign papers that will finally evict whatever remains inside. To survive, Oscar must return what was taken—a child's music box holding the original deed and a name no one has spoken since—before Marisol signs, even though doing so means surrendering the only home and the only family of ghosts Oscar has ever had. In the end, Oscar gives back the room, joins the found family on the other side of the glass, and the house stands empty at last, its mirrors running exactly on time.
about_author: Juniper Eriksen is the pen name of a former night-shift radio producer from coastal Maine who spent years collecting listeners' stories about houses that refused to let them go. Lena and the Room is their second novel, written mostly between midnight and four a.m.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. During the broadcast, a caller describes her own funeral in detail; Oscar recognizes the voice as Edie Marsh, dead six days. The emotional beat is practiced denial—Oscar's calm on-air voice cracking only after the sign-off.

chapters.title: The Second Behind
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At home, Oscar notices the bathroom mirror reflecting a raised hand one beat late. Testing it with a metronome confirms the lag. The beat is dread disguised as scientific curiosity.

chapters.title: House Rules
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Flashback to 2009: how Oscar inherited the house from Aunt Ruth, who left a list of rules taped inside a kitchen cabinet. Rule seven: never answer if someone knocks using your own rhythm. The beat is uneasy nostalgia.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. More dead listeners call in, each asking not for help but for Oscar to 'keep the light on.' Station manager Dev notices the show's ratings spiking among the recently bereaved. Beat: guilt and the first hint that Oscar's role is custodial.

chapters.title: The Woman at the Door
chapters.summary: Marisol Vane's POV. A lawyer's letter brings Marisol to the Ashgrove house; she claims her grandmother's family lived here until 1974 and something of theirs was never returned. Oscar turns her away. Beat: two kinds of loneliness meeting at a threshold.

chapters.title: What Ruth Knew
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Searching the attic, Oscar finds Ruth's journals describing the mirror lag in 1974—the year the previous family vanished mid-move—and a sketch of a music box. Beat: the collapse of fifteen years of explanations.

chapters.title: Lena
chapters.summary: The mirror's POV, rendered as fragmented reflection-narration. A small figure appears in the glass, waiting a full second behind everything, mouthing a name: Lena. Beat: eerie tenderness.

chapters.title: Papers
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol obtains probate documents showing the house was deeded under a false name in 1974, signed by someone who 'wasn't there.' Her lawyer urges speed. Beat: determination sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: Static
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. On air, every caller speaks in unison, asking Oscar to open the box before Friday. The station's transmitter fails; only Oscar hears the rest. Beat: terror braided with obligation.

chapters.title: The Knocking
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Someone knocks at 3 a.m. using Oscar's own signature rhythm. Oscar nearly opens the door; the mirror shows a second-Oscar already standing outside. Beat: the self turning uncanny.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Album
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol finds photos of the 1974 move: the family carrying out furniture while a girl clutches an empty spot where a music box should be. The girl is labeled 'Lena.' Beat: grief for a relative she never met.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The dead callers begin appearing in the house—not menacing, but domestic, setting three places at the table, warming a chair. Oscar realizes he has been less alone than he admitted. Beat: warmth curdling into dependence.

chapters.title: Dev Comes Over
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Worried about Oscar, Dev visits and sees nothing wrong—except he counts five chairs at a table set for two. He leaves shaken and stops returning calls. Beat: isolation tightening around Oscar.

chapters.title: The Price of Staying
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar understands the household will keep him forever, comfortable and reflected, if he does nothing. The mirror shows an older, grayer Oscar already living there. Beat: the seduction of belonging versus survival.

chapters.title: Signing Day Approaches
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Papers are scheduled for Friday. Marisol dreams of the house calling her by name and wakes with dirt under her fingernails. Beat: dread of inheritance.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The final journal page reveals Ruth took the music box in 1974 to keep the room 'for us,' trapping Lena's family half-in, half-out. Ruth's last line: 'Return it or become it.' Beat: horror at complicity across generations.

chapters.title: The Room Behind the Glass
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar steps through the lagging mirror into the held breath of 1974: a living room frozen mid-farewell, Lena waiting with empty hands. Beat: awe and heartbreak.

chapters.title: Friday
chapters.summary: Alternating Oscar/Marisol. As Marisol's pen touches paper, the house begins closing like a throat. Oscar calls the station one last time and asks the dead to hold the door. Beat: race against a signature.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar returns the music box to Lena's hands; the deed burns, the false name unwrites itself, and the frozen family finishes leaving. Lena says thank you by giving Oscar her place in the reflection. Beat: sacrifice offered and accepted.

chapters.title: Sign Here
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol signs—but the papers now transfer an empty house, honestly titled. She feels the building exhale. Beat: release.

chapters.title: On Time
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, from inside the glass. Oscar raises a hand; the mirror answers instantly now. The dead callers wave from the warm room behind. Beat: bittersweet belonging achieved at the price of the living world.

chapters.title: Keep the Light On
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Marisol's POV. Months later, Marisol lives in the house, keeps a lamp burning in the window, and sometimes hears a familiar voice reading the weather through the static. Beat: quiet peace, and the suggestion that some families persist.
